title: The upgrade stand and its roll
summary: The stand you buy upgrades from in R.E.P.O. is a machine of its own: it has a button you grab, a hatch that opens onto a compartment, a build-up with its own light and stages, a roller with start, rolling and settle curves, a reroll, and a fire it can break out into.
body: The upgrade stand is a machine rather than a shop counter. It has a button you grab, a hatch, a compartment the upgrade sits in and a check for whether the upgrade is inside its box, so what you buy is rolled out of the stand instead of being handed over.

A roll has stages of its own. There are separate curves for the shake as the roll starts, for the roll itself and for the shake as it settles, with a start sound, a loop while it rolls and a sound for the end.
The hatch is animated and loud. It has its own curve, a sound for opening and a different one for closing, plus separate impact sounds for each, and particles of its own.
There is a reroll as well. It has sounds for starting, for each tick, for settling and for finishing, and the compartment it uses carries hurt colliders of its own.

The build-up is sounded and the hatch can hurt. The beep while it builds up and the squeak as the final roll settles are sounds of their own, and the hatch carries a hurt collider, which is why reaching into a moving stand is a physical thing rather than a menu.

The button is a whole object. It has a renderer with a normal material and a deny material, a curve for the press and another for a refusal, springs for its rotation, and sounds for pressing, refusing and twisting up and down.
The stand builds up before it rolls. It has stages to go through, a build-up light, an intro curve and an outro curve, build-up particles, a loop sound and a length for the build-up.

It can catch fire. A fire light, a hurt collider for the fire, a looping fire particle, rubble for the button, a break particle and a break sound all belong to the stand, which is why a failed roll is more than a message.
The parts move on springs. The whole mesh carries a rotation spring and a position spring, and the button has one of its own, so the stand reacts rather than switching between poses.
It also powers itself on and off. There are sounds for the stand being on and off and for a light going out, a curve for a flickering fade, and rolling particles that belong to the roll.
The pictures beside this entry are the game's own: the colour artwork for the stand's button, which carries the arrow mark, and for its roller.
What this entry does not tell you: what an upgrade costs, what any of them does, or how the odds of a roll work. We have not verified those numbers, so we do not print them.

facts.claim: The stand has a button you grab, a hatch, a compartment for the upgrade and a check for the upgrade being inside its box.

facts.claim: There is a reroll with sounds for starting, ticking, settling and ending, and a compartment with hurt colliders.

facts.claim: The mesh and the button each carry springs of their own.
